column1: # do not include extraneous commas in the fields - use semicolons if needed
'Application' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: Top layer of the OSI model

column1: 'Presentation' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: Second layer of the OSI model

column1: 'Session' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: Whether it be a VPN tunnel; SSL session; or a remote desktop session; this layer is responsible for establishing; managing; and terminating sessions between applications

column1: 'Transport' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: Handles port numbers to get data to the right application; TCP adds reliability/ordering/3 way handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK); UDP doesn't.

column1: 'Network' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: This is where IP addressing and routing occurs

column1: 'Data Link' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: This layer is responsible for node-to-node data transfer and error detection

column1: 'Physical' is what # on the OSI model?
column3: This layer is responsible for the physical connection between devices and the transmission of raw bit streams over a physical medium

column1: Alternate acronym for MAC addresses?
column3: Data Link Control; apparently refers to the exact same thing

column1: On what OSI layer would a packet would get 'fragmented'?
column3: Fragmentation of packets occurs at the Network layer if the packet size exceeds the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of the network

column1: On what OSI layer would data 'segmentation' occur?
column3: Segmentation of data occurs at the Transport layer to break down large messages into smaller segments for transmission

column1: On what OSI layer would Tunneling protocols be used?
column3: Tunneling protocols (such as PPTP; L2TP; and GRE) operate at the Session layer.

column1: IDS and IPS - what does the I stand for?
column3: Intrusion Detection System (IDS) and Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) monitor network traffic for suspicions activity and can take action. May be integrated into NG firewalls.

column1: One server goes down but users do not notice a change; what is probably in place?
column3: Load balancers distribute incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server becomes overwhelmed; can tell if server down and direct traffic elsewhere.

column1: Network storage devices: Block Level Access\File Level Access (Acronyms)?
column3: SAN (Storage Area Network) provides block-level access to storage devices and clients OS manages the filesystem; NAS (Network Attached Storage) abstracts the file system for you and provides file-level access.

column1: What OSI layer does an access point operate at?
column3: Bridges wireless clients to the wired network based on MAC addresses; same fundamental job as a switch just over radio. (802.11 Wireless <----> 802.3 Wired)

column1: Uses local caching servers to speed up delivery of data and content to users? (Acronym)
column3: Content Delivery Network (CDN) are geographically distributed caching servers that duplicate the data locally to increase speed of delivery to users

column1: Single device that is often central connection point for VPN traffic; high-volume encryption/decryption; often integrated into firewalls?
column3: A concentrator or head-end device acts as a central connection point for all users or branch offices connecting to a VPN; can also be software.

column1: Default TTL for Mac/Linux? (hops)
column3: Default Time To Live (TTL) value for packets on Mac and Linux systems is 64 hops

column1: Default TTL for Windows? (hops)
column3: Default Time To Live (TTL) value for packets on Windows systems is 128 hops

column1: Acronym related to replacing dedicated hardware appliances (firewall; router; etc..) with software versions?
column3: Network Function Virtualization - runs network functions as software/VMs instead of dedicated physical hardware. Likely happening in most cloud environments.

column1: VPC Meaning?
column3: A pool of resources created in a public cloud; often connected via a 'transit gateway' (cloud router) to other VPCs or on-premises networks(?)

column1: RIP = ? ? Protocol?
column3: Oldest/simplest routing protocol; picks paths by hop count only; maxes out at 15 hops; mostly outdated; if used at all it's typically inside one organizations network.

column1: BGP = ? ? Protocol?
column3: Routes between separate large networks/ISPs; runs the entire internet at the largest scale.

column1: OSPF Meaning?
column3: Link-state protocol; picks paths by cost/bandwidth not just hop count; common for routing inside one organization's network.

column1: Uses the slash notation (eg /25) to allow networks to be split into smaller subnets (acronym)?
column3: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) allows for more efficient use of IP address space by allowing variable-length subnet masks (VLSM) and the use of slash notation to represent network prefixes.

column1: Used to control cloud traffic at a high level; often across multiple subnets (Comptia term; acronym)
column3: Network Security List (NSL) - shown as applying broadly to everything in one or more subnets; different cloud providers do handle this differently and have more specific terms

column1: Used to control cloud traffic at a more granular level; able to apply to specific devices (Comptia term; acronym)
column3: Network Security Group (NSG) - able to apply to specific devices in a subnet; or presumably to specific subnets themselves (maybe this depends on the cloud provider - for the test just remember this is specific devices))

column1: Software that sits between other pieces of software; handling communication and integration between them
column3: Examples include message queues; application servers; and web servers; API gateways; Authentication/session management layers (managed by the provider in a PaaS environment)

column1: Which layer 4 protocol does not have flow control?
column3: User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is a connectionless rotocol used for fast; real-time data like video streaming or gaming where lost packets are less important than speed

column1: The range for Dynamic/Ephemeral ports is (normally) #-#?
column3: Dynamic or ephemeral ports are typically assigned by the operating system for short-lived connections and are in the range of 49152 to 65535

column1: The range for Registered ports is (normally) #-#?
column3: Registered ports are assigned by IANA for specific services and applications and are in the range of 1024 to 49151 (sometimes included in ephemeral range)

column1: The range for Well Known ports is (normally) #-#?
column3: Well-known ports are mostly reserved for system or widely used services and are in the range of 0 to 1023 (the usual suspects)

column1: A technique that combines multiple signals or data streams into a single composite signal
column3: Multiplexing is a technique that combines multiple signals or data streams into a single composite signal for transmission over a shared medium; examples include Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) and Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM)

column1: Port: FTP Data Connection
column3: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) uses port 20 for data transfer in active mode (versus passive mode; which uses a random port in the dynamic/ephemeral range instead).

column1: Port: FTP Control Connection
column3: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) uses port 21 for control commands and responses between the client and server e.g. USER/PASS for login; CWD to change directory; LIST to view files; RETR/STOR to trigger downloads/uploads.

column1: Port: SSH
column3: Secure Shell (SSH) uses port 22 for secure remote login and command execution; also used for secure file transfers via SCP (Secure Copy Protocol) and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol).

column1: Rides on top of SSH for simple file copying
column3: Secure Copy Protocol (SCP) is a simple file transfer protocol that rides on top of SSH and uses port 22 for secure file copying between hosts.

column1: Rides on top of SSH for more advanced file transfers
column3: SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) is a more advanced file transfer protocol that rides on top of SSH and uses port 22 for secure file transfers with additional features like directory listings and file management.

column1: Port: Telnet
column3: Telnet uses port 23 for unencrypted remote login and command execution; it is considered insecure and has largely been replaced by SSH. (Telnet sends everything — including login credentials — in plaintext)

column1: Port: Unencrypted SMTP
column3: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) uses port 25 for sending email messages between mail servers unencrypted (Always TCP)

column1: Port: SMTPS (Implicit SSL/TLS)
column3: SMTPS (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol Secure) uses port 465 for sending email messages securely over SSL/TLS; Encrypted from the start (TCP)

column1: Port: STARTTLS (Explicit SSL/TLS)
column3: STARTTLS is an extension to SMTP that allows for the upgrade of an existing unencrypted connection to a secure connection using SSL/TLS; typically uses port 587 for sending email securely. (TCP)

column1: Port: DNS
column3: Domain Name System (DNS) uses UDP port 53 for standard queries and TCP port 53 for larger transfers like zone transfers or DNSSEC responses; use nslookup (or Resolve-DnsName in PowerShell) on Windows; or dig on Linux/Mac; to query DNS info manually.

column1: Protocol/Ports: DHCP
column3: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) uses UDP port 67 for the server and UDP port 68 for the client; DHCP is used to automatically assign IP addresses and other network configuration parameters to devices on a network.

column1: Protocol/Port: TFTP
column3: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) uses UDP port 69 for simple file transfers; it is a lightweight version of FTP and does not provide authentication; encryption or directory browsing.

column1: Protocol/Ports: HTTP (Unsecure/Secure)
column3: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) uses TCP port 80 for unencrypted web traffic and TCP port 443 for HTTPS (traffic encrypted with SSL/TLS))

column1: Protocol/Port: NTP
column3: Network Time Protocol (NTP) uses UDP port 123 for synchronizing the clocks of computer systems/switches/routers/firewalls/etc..; sync is critical for log files/auth details/outages/kerberos auth/etc..

column1: Protocol/Port: SNMP
column3: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) uses UDP port 161 for a network management system to query device status and push configuration changes to managed devices (routers/switches/servers/etc.).

column1: Protocol/Port: SNMP Trap
column3: SNMP Trap uses UDP port 162 for devices to send unsolicited notifications (traps) to a network management system about significant events or changes in status.

column1: Protocol/Port: LDAP
column3: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) uses TCP port 389 for querying and modifying directory services; often used for authentication and authorization in enterprise environments.

column1: Protocol/Port: LDAPS
column3: LDAPS (LDAP over SSL/TLS) uses TCP port 636 for secure communication with directory services; it encrypts LDAP traffic using SSL/TLS to protect sensitive information like user credentials and directory data.

column1: Protocol/Port/Alternate (older) Acronym: SMB
column3: Server Message Block (SMB) uses TCP port 445 for file and printer sharing in Windows networks; Common Internet File System (CIFS) is older now-deprecated dialect of SMB that had security vulnerabilities (essentially SMB1)

column1: Protocol/Port: Syslog
column3: Syslog uses UDP port 514 for sending log messages from devices to a centralized log server; it is commonly used for monitoring and troubleshooting network devices and systems.

column1: Protocol/Port: Syslog (Secure/TLS)
column3: Syslog over TLS uses TCP port 6514 for sending log messages securely and reliably to a centralized log server; unlike standard UDP syslog (514) this version guarantees delivery and encrypts the log data in transit.

column1: Protocol/Port RDP
column3: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) uses TCP port 3389 for remote access to Windows desktops and servers; There are RDP clients for Mac/Linux/Others as well; RDP is often used in conjunction with VPNs for secure remote access.

column1: Dedicated software that Collects/Correlates Syslog log files and generates Alerts/Reports (Acronym)
column3: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) is not a standalone device itself; it is software that runs on a dedicated server; VM; or cloud platform; and pulls logs from many sources across a network (firewalls; servers; endpoints) often via syslog.

column1: What is the control protocol commonly used to manage VoIP connections?
column3: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is a signaling protocol used to establish; modify; and terminate multimedia sessions such as voice and video calls over IP networks; often used in VoIP systems.

column1: Protocol/Port: SIP
column3: Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is used to initiate; manage; and terminate VoIP calls (signaling only; not the actual voice data); can run over TCP or UDP depending on implementation.

column1: Protocol/Port: SIPS
column3: SIPS (SIP Secure) is SIP signaling encrypted with TLS; always uses TCP since a reliable connection is needed to establish the TLS handshake.

column1: What protocol carries the actual audio/video data during a VoIP call (after SIP sets it up)?
column3: Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries the actual media (audio/video) data during a call over UDP; it uses timestamps and sequence numbers to help reconstruct the stream in order; but does not request retransmission of lost packets like TCP would.

column1: Protocol associated with Pings?
column3: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) is used for network diagnostics and error reporting; used by the ping command to test connectivity between devices; TTL/Unreachable information as well (Not TCP or UDP; separate protocol on top of IP)

column1: Protocol used to encapsulate packets/used for tunneling?
column3: Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) is a tunneling protocol that encapsulates packets of one protocol within another protocol; often used to create VPNs or to transport non-IP traffic over an IP network. Does not do the encryption itself.

column1: Device/function that terminates and manages multiple simultaneous VPN connections?
column3: Can be a small office firewall configured to accept remote VPN connections or a dedicated large-scale appliance for handling many tunnels (e.g. site-to-site VPNs across many locations); the term describes the function; not a specific product category.

column1: The two core IPSec Protocols? (Acronym/Acronym)
column3: Authentication Header (AH) provides authentication and integrity for IP packets; Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) provides confidentiality (encryption); authentication; and integrity for IP packets; both are used in IPSec VPNs.

column1: Protocol that handles key exchange/negotiation in IPSec VPNs; almost always present? (Acronym/Protocol/Port)
column3: Internet Key Exchange (IKE) establishes and manages security associations (SAs) in IPsec VPNs; negotiates encryption algorithms and keys before ESP/AH can operate.

column1: SA Meaning (Related to IKE)
column3: A Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters that define how two devices will communicate securely using IPSec; it includes encryption algorithms; keys; and other security settings negotiated during the IKE process.

column1: If Encapsulation Security Payload (ESP) has to go through a NAT device what protocol/port is used?
column3: It is encapsulated in UDP packets using port 4500 to allow it to traverse the NAT device; this is known as NAT-T (NAT Traversal).

column1: Piece at the (very) end of an ESP packet?
column3: The Integrity Check Value (ICV) is a cryptographic checksum at the end of an ESP packet that ensures the integrity of the packet; it allows the receiving device to verify that the packet has not been tampered with during transit. (In AH it is part of the AH Header)

column1: The protocol devices use to say "I want to join this multicast group
column3: IGMP
column4: Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by devices to join or leave multicast groups; it allows routers to manage multicast traffic and ensure that only interested devices receive the multicast streams. (IP Protocol 2)

column1: Multicast traffic IP range (just the first octets) x-x
column3: IPv4 multicast uses 224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255; the range is independent of your normal network address

column1: Network routing method that picks the best recipient among multiple with the same IP?
column3: Anycast is a network routing style where multiple devices share the same IP address; the network routes traffic to the nearest or best-performing device based on routing metrics; commonly used for content delivery networks (CDNs) and DNS servers.

column1: Wireless Standard Designation (#)/The organization that created it:
column3: The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) is the organization that develops and maintains the 802.11 wireless networking standards; Standards committee IEEE 802 is responsible for LAN/MAN standards

column1: What does the M in LAN/MAN stand for?
column3: PAN = Personal Area Network; LAN = Local Area Network; MAN = Metropolitan Area Network; WAN = Wide Area Network

column1: The letters for Wi-Fi 4/5/6?
Letter/Nominal Speed for WiFi-4 (per 20 Mhz stream)/theoretical maximum
column3: Wi-Fi 4 (802.11n) has a nominal speed of 72 Mbps per 20 MHz stream; with MIMO and multiple streams it can reach a theoretical maximum of 600 Mbps.

column1: Letter/Nominal Speed for WiFi-5 (per 80 Mhz stream)/theoretical maximum
column3: Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) has a nominal speed of 433 Mbps per 80 MHz spatial stream; with 8 spatial streams and 160 MHz channels it can reach a theoretical maximum of 6933 Mbps.

column1: Letter/Nominal Speed for WiFi-6 (per 80 Mhz stream)/theoretical maximum
column3: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) has a nominal speed of about 600 Mbps per 80 MHz spatial stream; with 8 spatial streams and 160 MHz channels it can reach a theoretical maximum of 9608 Mbps. (6E is where 6Ghz starts)

column1: Letter/Nominal Speed for WiFi-7 (per 160 Mhz stream)/theoretical maximum
column3: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) has a nominal speed of about 1376 Mbps per 160 MHz spatial stream; with 16 spatial streams using 320 MHz channels it can reach a theoretical maximum of 46120 Mbps.

column1: DFS Meaning? (Just type the DF)
column3: Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) is a mechanism that allows Wi-Fi devices to detect radar signals and switch to a different channel to avoid interference; it is required for certain 5 GHz channels in many countries.

column1: Nominal speeds for 802.11 a/b/g
Acronyms for 2G cellular networks in US (AT&T+T-Mobile/Verizon+Sprint)
column3: GSM = Global System for Mobile Communications; CDMA = Code Division Multiple Access; GSM evolved toward UMTS for 3G; CDMA evolved toward CDMA2000/EV-DO (Evolution-Data Optimized)

column1: 4G/LTE theoretical download rate
column3: Professor Messer uses approximately 150 Mbps for 4G/LTE

column1: LTE-A theoretical download rate
column3: LTE-Advanced is an improved version of LTE; Messer uses approximately 300 Mbps

column1: Acronym for the technology that uses multiple antennas for multiple spatial streams
column3: Multiple Input Multiple Output (MIMO) uses multiple antennas at the transmitter and receiver; 2x2 is common; 4x4 can provide higher data rates. (MU-MIMO for multiple users)

column1: 5G theoretical max download rate (Gbps)/expected speed (Mbit/s from messers slide)
column3: 5G theoretical maximum download rate is 10 Gbps; actual expected speeds are typically in the range of 100-900 Mbps depending on network conditions and deployment.

column1: Satellite Networking common speeds (Mbps) down/up (from messers slide)
column3: Satellite internet connections typically have download speeds around 100 Mbps and upload speeds around 5 Mbps; latency is usually higher due to the long distance signals must travel to and from satellites.

column1: Latency for Satellite Networking (ms-round trip) Traditional/Starlink Current/Starlink Future
column3: Traditional geostationary satellite: Messer says 250 up and down so 500 round trip; Starlink current is about 40 ms; Starlink future is expected to be around 20 (Messer says higher frequencies 2 Ghz+)

column1: Types of Satellites (Traditional/Starlink)
column3: Traditional satellites are typically in Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) at about 35786 km above the equator; Starlink satellites are in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) at about 550 km (below 2000 anyway) above the Earth.

column1: Ethernet Standard Designation (#)/The organization that created it
column3: The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) is the organization that develops and maintains the 802.3 Ethernet networking standards; Standards committee IEEE 802 is responsible for LAN/MAN standards

column1: Gigabit Ethernet standard that goes over Fiber (short wavelength)?
column3: 1000BASE-SX is a Gigabit Ethernet standard that uses short-wavelength (850 nm) multimode fiber optic cables for high-speed data transmission over relatively short distances (up to 550 meters).

column1: Gigabit Ethernet standard that goes over Fiber (long wavelength)?
column3: 1000BASE-LX is a Gigabit Ethernet standard that uses long-wavelength (1310 nm) single-mode fiber optic cables for high-speed data transmission over longer distances (up to 10 kilometers).

column1: OM meaning (regarding fiber optic cable)
column3: OM = Optical Multimode; a category of multimode fiber optic cable. OM followed by a number (e.g.; OM1; OM2; OM3; OM4; OM5) indicates the cable's performance characteristics and maximum data transmission distance.

column1: Acronyms for the two types of fiber (Shorter Distance/Longer Distance)
column3: MMF = Multimode Fiber (850 nm commonly); SMF = Single-mode Fiber (1310 or 1550 nm commonly); MMF is used for shorter distances; SMF is used for longer distances.

column1: The even longer Fiber type designations (40km/70-80km/fiber mode ??F)
column3: EX = Extended reach (40 km; 1310 nm); ZX = Very long reach (70-80 km; 1550 nm); both use Single-mode Fiber (SMF).

column1: What is Fiber immune to that Copper is not?
column3: Fiber is immune to electromagnetic interference (EMI) because they use light; or as Messer puts it do not have RF signals (while Ethernet uses electrical signals that can be affected by EMI; hence twisting; shielding; etc.)
